title: Compound words: reading Swedish one block at a time
title_target: Här har vi ett långt ord för allt.
goal: Take long Swedish compounds apart from the end, recognize the linking letters that glue them together, and stress them the Swedish way.
bekal: you can break a long word like *arbetsmiljöverket* into its parts and guess its meaning
you know when Swedish adds a linking *-s-*, *-e-*, *-u-* or *-o-*, and when it adds nothing
you can stress a compound on its first part and know why *grönsak* is not *grön sak*
wave: Go back to Unit 2 (Strong verbs by vowel family): many compounds hide a strong verb (*skrivbord* from *skriva*, *sittplats* from *sitta*, *dricksvatten* from *dricka*). Find the verb in each, then say its three forms aloud: *skriva, skrev, skrivit*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Arbetsmiljöenkäten
dialogs.intro: Karin has emailed the whole team a questionnaire about the work environment. Dian opens it at her desk and gets stuck on the very first word. Leila rolls her chair over to help.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Leila, kan du hjälpa mig? Det här ordet tar aldrig slut.
lines.id: Leila, can you help me? This word never ends.
lines.literal: Leila, can you help me? this here word-the takes never end.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Vilket då? Visa. Aha, ”arbetsmiljöenkät”. Det är bara tre ord som sitter ihop.
lines.id: Which one? Show me. Aha, "arbetsmiljöenkät". It's just three words stuck together.
lines.literal: which then? show. aha, work-environment-survey. it is only three words that sit together.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Arbete, miljö och enkät. Men var kommer s:et ifrån?
lines.id: Work, environment and survey. But where does the s come from?
lines.literal: work, environment and survey. but where comes s-the from?

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Det är ett så kallat fogs. Det limmar ihop delarna, ungefär som ett bindestreck man kan höra.
lines.id: That's what's called a linking s. It glues the parts together, a bit like a hyphen you can hear.
lines.literal: it is a so called joint-s. it glues together parts-the, roughly like a hyphen one can hear.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Okej. Och vad vill de veta i enkäten?
lines.id: OK. And what do they want to know in the questionnaire?
lines.literal: okay. and what want they know in survey-the?

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Allt om arbetsplatsen. Hur din skrivbordsstol funkar, om du har ett höj- och sänkbart skrivbord, sådana saker.
lines.id: Everything about the workplace. How your desk chair works, whether you have a height-adjustable desk, that kind of thing.
lines.literal: all about work-place-the. how your desk-chair works, if you have a raise- and lowerable desk, such things.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Min stol är faktiskt hemsk. Jag får ont i ryggen efter lunch.
lines.id: My chair is actually awful. My back starts hurting after lunch.
lines.literal: my chair is actually awful. I get pain in back-the after lunch.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Skriv det! Och glöm inte frågan om friskvårdsbidraget längst ner.
lines.id: Write that down! And don't forget the question about the wellness allowance at the bottom.
lines.literal: write it! and forget not question-the about fresh-care-contribution-the furthest down.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Friskvårdsbidraget? Nu blev det tre delar igen.
lines.id: The wellness allowance? Now it's three parts again.
lines.literal: fresh-care-contribution-the? now became it three parts again.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Frisk, vård, bidrag. Företaget betalar till exempel en del av ditt gymkort.
lines.id: Healthy, care, allowance. The company pays part of your gym membership, for example.
lines.literal: healthy, care, contribution. company-the pays for example a part of your gym-card.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vilken förmån! Det har vi inte hemma i Indonesien.
lines.id: What a perk! We don't have that back home in Indonesia.
lines.literal: what benefit! that have we not home in Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Välkommen till Sverige. Här har vi ett långt ord för allt.
lines.id: Welcome to Sweden. Here we have a long word for everything.
lines.literal: welcome to Sweden. here have we a long word for all.

notes: **Arbetsmiljöenkät** — read it from the **end**. The last part tells you what the thing *is* (*enkät*, a questionnaire); everything in front only describes it: a questionnaire about the environment of work. Say it as one word with one main stress at the start: **AHR-bets-mil-yö-en-keht**.

**Fogs** — the "joint s" (*en fog* is a joint between two boards). It is not a plural or a possessive, just glue. Notice that *arbete* loses its final *-e* before the *s*: *arbet**s**miljö*, *arbet**s**plats*.

**Skrivbordsstol** — *skriv* (write) + *bord* (table) = *skrivbord* (desk); + *s* + *stol* (chair) = desk chair. The double *s* is simply the fogs meeting the *s* of *stol*. Say **SKREEV-boods-stool**.

**Höj- och sänkbart** — the hyphen tells you that a part is shared: *höjbart och sänkbart* (raisable and lowerable). English does the same in "pre- and post-war". *Bart* has the *-t* because *skrivbord* is an *ett*-word.

**Friskvårdsbidrag** — most Swedish employers give staff a yearly, tax-free sum toward exercise: a gym card, swimming, yoga, a floorball club. It is one of the first perks Swedes mention when they compare jobs. Pronounced **FRISK-vohds-bee-drahg**, with *rd* losing its *r*.
**Vilken förmån!** — *vilken/vilket/vilka* + noun makes an exclamation, like English "What a…!": *Vilken utsikt!* (What a view!), *Vilket väder!* (What weather!). No article is needed after it.

grammars.title: How a compound is built
body: A Swedish compound is two or more words written together as one. The **last** part is the head: it decides the meaning, the gender (*en* or *ett*) and the plural. The parts in front only narrow it down. *Ett skrivbord* is an *ett*-word because *bord* is, but *en skrivbordsstol* is an *en*-word because *stol* is.
after: Only the last part takes the definite ending or the plural: *spårvagnshållplats**en***, *tandborst**ar***. Nothing inside the word changes.

grammars.title: The glue: -s-, -e-, -u-, -o- or nothing
body: Between the parts Swedish sometimes adds a linking letter. There are tendencies rather than iron rules, but the ones below cover most of what you will meet.

head: Glue
When
Examples
rows: when the first part is itself a compound
after some short words, by habit
a few verbs and older words

after: The most reliable rule is the first *-s-* row: if the first part is **already** a compound, an *-s-* almost always follows. *Vagn* + *förare* gives *vagnförare* (tram driver), but *spårvagn* + *förare* gives *spårvagn**s**förare*. Trust the rule more than your ear at first.
A first part that already ends in *-s* gets no extra *s*: *buss* + *hållplats* = *busshållplats*, *hus* + *båt* = *husbåt*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ordspel på spårvagnen
dialogs.intro: Thursday after work. Oskar has met Dian at Lindholmen, and they take the tram together toward Majorna. To pass the time, Oskar suggests a very Swedish game: building longer and longer words.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Ska vi spela ett ordspel medan vi åker? Jag säger ett ord, och du bygger vidare.
lines.id: Shall we play a word game while we ride? I say a word, and you build on it.
lines.literal: shall we play a word-game while we ride? I say a word, and you build further.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Okej, börja du.
lines.id: OK, you start.
lines.literal: okay, begin you.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Spårvagn. Din tur!
lines.id: Tram. Your turn!
lines.literal: track-wagon. your turn!

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Spårvagnshållplats! Med fogs, eller hur?
lines.id: Tram stop! With a linking s, right?
lines.literal: track-wagon-s-stop! with joint-s, or how?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Snyggt. Spårvagnshållplatsskylt.
lines.id: Nice one. Tram-stop sign.
lines.literal: neat. track-wagon-s-stop-sign.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nu blir det löjligt. Hur uttalar man ens det?
lines.id: Now it's getting ridiculous. How do you even pronounce that?
lines.literal: now becomes it ridiculous. how pronounces one even it?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Huvudbetoningen ligger på första delen, SPÅR. Resten går liksom nedåt.
lines.id: The main stress is on the first part, SPÅR. The rest sort of slopes down.
lines.literal: head-stress-the lies on first part-the, TRACK. rest-the goes sort-of downward.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Men Göteborg då? Där ligger betoningen ju sist.
lines.id: But what about Göteborg? There the stress comes last.
lines.literal: but Göteborg then? there lies stress-the as-you-know last.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Ortnamn är undantag. Vanliga sammansatta ord betonas alltid i början.
lines.id: Place names are exceptions. Ordinary compound words are always stressed at the start.
lines.literal: place-names are exceptions. ordinary put-together words are-stressed always in beginning-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Grönsak, alltså. Inte grön sak.
lines.id: So: vegetable. Not a green thing.
lines.literal: green-thing, so. not green thing.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Exakt! Och skriv aldrig isär dem. En sjuk sköterska är något helt annat än en sjuksköterska.
lines.id: Exactly! And never write them apart. A sick nurse is something completely different from a nurse.
lines.literal: exactly! and write never apart them. a sick nurse is something whole other than a sick-nurse.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nästa hållplats är min. Vi fortsätter spelet på måndag!
lines.id: The next stop is mine. We'll carry on with the game on Monday!
lines.literal: next stop is mine. we continue game-the on Monday!

notes: **Spårvagn** — *spår* (track) + *vagn* (car, carriage): a tram. Göteborg has one of the largest tram networks in Northern Europe, and locals simply call it *spårvagnen* or *vagnen*. Pronounced **SPOHR-vahngn**; in the compound the *-s-* follows: **SPOHR-vahngns-hol-plahts**.

**Bygga vidare** — *vidare* (further, on) turns many verbs into "keep doing": *bygga vidare* (build on), *läsa vidare* (read on), *gå vidare* (move on). **Snyggt** (literally "good-looking") is everyday praise among friends: Nice one!

**Huvudbetoningen** — a compound has its main stress on the first part and a weaker stress on the last part, and it always gets **tone 2**, the rising-falling-rising melody. That melody is what tells a listener "this is one word".

**Göteborg** — place names follow their own rules. The city is stressed at the end, and locals say something close to **yö-teh-BORY**, with the final *g* turning into a *y*. *Stockholm* (**STOK-holm**), on the other hand, behaves like an ordinary compound.

**Grönsak, inte grön sak** — the same two words, two meanings: **GRÖN-sahk** (vegetable, one stress, tone 2) and **grön SAHK** (a green thing, two stresses). Stress and spelling go together: one word in writing, one main stress in speech.

**Skriv aldrig isär dem** — writing a compound as two words is called *särskrivning*, and Swedes love to collect examples of it on menus and signs. A *sjuksköterska* (**HWÜK-hwö-tesh-kah**) is a nurse; *en sjuk sköterska* is a nurse who happens to be ill.

grammars.title: One word or two: stress and spelling decide
body: Because a compound has a single main stress, joining or separating two words can change the meaning completely. Each pair below is a classic. In the left column the words are written together and stressed once; in the right column they are two words with two stresses.

head: Compound (one stress)
Two words (two stresses)
rows: **en kort film** = a film that is short
**en sjuk sköterska** = a nurse who is ill

after: The last two are the famous menu and sign mistakes. Notice that a compound with an adjective first (*grönsak*, *kortfilm*) never takes adjective endings inside: *grönsaker*, *kortfilmen*, never *gröna saker* in the sense of vegetables.

sections.title: Reading monster words from the back

blocks.text: Official Swedish is full of words that look impossible at first glance. They are not harder than short words, only longer. Use the same four steps every time, and you will be able to read the name of every Swedish government agency by the end of this unit.

items: **Find the last word you recognize.** That is the head: *-verket* (the agency), *-kassan* (the fund), *-föreningen* (the association).
**Peel off the glue.** An *-s-*, *-e-*, *-u-* or *-o-* just before a new part is only glue.
**Work leftward,** one block at a time, until nothing is left.
**Read the meaning back to front** in English: *arbets|miljö|verket* = the agency for the environment of work.

head: Word
Parts
Meaning
rows: the Social Insurance Agency (lit. insurance fund)

blocks.title: Agencies and their tails
items: **-styrelsen**: Transportstyrelsen, Socialstyrelsen (National Board of Health and Welfare).
You will meet several of them again in Unit 19, when Dian deals with Swedish bureaucracy.

sections.title: Writing compounds: together, with a hyphen, or apart

blocks.text: The default is simple: **write compounds as one word**, however long. Swedish uses a hyphen in only a handful of cases, and English-style separate writing is always wrong for a compound.

head: Use a hyphen when…
Example
rows: the first part is an abbreviation or a letter
the first part is a number in digits
a part is shared between two words
höj- och sänkbar, in- och utgång

blocks.text: In speech, the same rule appears as melody: if you hear one main stress and the rise-fall-rise of tone 2, you are hearing one word. Practice by saying these aloud as single words: *spårvagnshållplats*, *skrivbordsstol*, *friskvårdsbidrag*, *arbetsmiljöenkät*.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 10
items: Dian says *Nästa hållplats är min*, with no definite ending after *nästa*. Remember the rule from Unit 10: no double definiteness after *nästa*, *förra*, *samma*.

After *nästa* and *samma* the noun keeps its bare form: *nästa spårvagn*, *samma skrivbordsstol*, *nästa enkät*. After *förra* it takes the end article: *förra veckan*, *förra året*. None of them takes *den* or *det* in front.
Say six phrases aloud with compounds from this unit: *nästa hållplats*, *samma arbetsplats*, *nästa arbetsmiljöenkät*, *samma tandborste*, *förra veckan*, *förra spårvagnen*.

The tram stop is over there.
Compound words are stressed at the beginning.

ett dagsljus — ett gatunamn — en säkerhetskontroll — en skolgård — en tidningsartikel
Ortnamn är ofta undantag. — Företaget betalar en del av gymkortet. — Nästa hållplats är min. — Här sitter tre ord ihop. — Jag får ont i ryggen efter lunch.

Jag behöver en ny skrivbordsstol. — Spårvagnshållplatsen ligger där borta. — Grönsaker är nyttiga. — Sammansatta ord betonas i början. — Min syster är sjuksköterska.
